essay_prompts.prompt: Explain why being good at mental arithmetic is still useful in a world full of calculators.
Describe a time when numbers helped you make a better decision. What did you learn?
Should every adult understand basic percentages? Give reasons and examples.
Explain a simple mathematical idea to someone who is afraid of maths.
Write about a word or phrase you love and explain why it is powerful.
Is it more important to speak correctly or to speak confidently? Argue your view.
Describe a book, article or speech that changed the way you think.
Write a letter to your younger self about the value of reading.
Why is learning a second language worth the effort for an adult? Give three reasons.
Describe a place where French is spoken that you would like to visit, and why.
What is the hardest part of learning a new language, and how would you overcome it?
How can learning French help someone in their career in Africa or elsewhere?
Which scientific discovery has had the biggest effect on daily life? Defend your choice.
Should governments spend more money on space exploration or on problems at home?
Explain how technology has changed the way people learn.
Describe the steps you would take to test a claim you saw on social media.
What makes a good leader? Use examples to support your answer.
Explain why young people should or should not take part in elections.
Describe the role of a free press in a healthy society.
Compare two ways a country can choose its leaders. Which do you think is fairer?
Explain how rising prices affect ordinary families, and what they can do about it.
Should a country produce most of what it needs or trade for it? Argue your view.
Describe how a small business can create jobs and help a community grow.
What is one economic change that would improve life in your country? Explain why.
Why is saving money difficult, and what habits make it easier?

items.title: What is inflation?
items.body: Inflation is a general rise in prices over time, so each unit of money buys less. It is often measured with a consumer price index (CPI), which tracks the cost of a typical basket of goods and services.

items.title: Supply and demand
items.body: When demand for something rises and supply stays the same, its price tends to rise. When supply rises and demand stays the same, the price tends to fall. The price where the two meet is called the equilibrium.

items.title: What GDP measures
items.body: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a given period, usually a year or a quarter. It is the most common measure of the size of an economy.

items.title: GDP per person
items.body: GDP per capita divides GDP by the population. It is a rough guide to average living standards, but it hides inequality: a few very rich people can raise the average while most people's incomes stay low.

items.title: Opportunity cost
items.body: The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative you give up. If you spend an evening working overtime, the opportunity cost might be time with family. Every choice has one.

items.title: What central banks do
items.body: A central bank manages a country's currency and money supply. One of its main tools is the interest rate: raising rates makes borrowing more expensive, which tends to slow spending and inflation.

items.title: Comparative advantage
items.body: Countries gain from trade when each specialises in what it produces at a lower opportunity cost than others, even if one country is better at everything. The idea is linked to the economist David Ricardo (1817).

items.title: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation
items.body: In 2008 Zimbabwe experienced one of the worst hyperinflations in history, with prices doubling roughly every day at its peak. The central bank printed a 100 trillion dollar note. The currency was abandoned in 2009.

items.title: What is a recession?
items.body: A recession is a significant, widespread fall in economic activity. A common rule of thumb is two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, though official bodies look at wider data such as jobs and incomes.

items.title: Exchange rates
items.body: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. When your currency weakens, imports cost more but your exports become cheaper for foreign buyers.

items.title: What is a tariff?
items.body: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. Governments use tariffs to raise money or protect local industries, but they usually make imported goods more expensive for consumers and can lead to retaliation.

items.title: Trade surplus and deficit
items.body: The balance of trade is a country's exports minus its imports. If it exports more than it imports, it has a trade surplus. If it imports more, it has a trade deficit.

items.title: Measuring unemployment
items.body: The unemployment rate is the share of people in the labour force who have no job but are available and looking for work. People not looking for work, such as full-time students, are not counted as unemployed.

items.title: What is a monopoly?
items.body: A monopoly exists when one company is the only seller of a product with no close substitutes. Without competition it can charge higher prices, which is why many countries have competition laws.

items.title: Price elasticity
items.body: Price elasticity of demand measures how much buying changes when price changes. Demand for essentials like salt barely changes (inelastic); demand for luxuries or items with substitutes changes a lot (elastic).

items.title: Scarcity
items.body: Scarcity is the basic economic problem: human wants are unlimited, but resources such as land, labour, time and money are limited. So people, businesses and governments must make choices.

items.title: The Wealth of Nations
items.body: Adam Smith published 'The Wealth of Nations' in 1776. It argued that division of labour and free markets create wealth, and introduced the famous 'invisible hand' idea. It is often called the first modern work of economics.

items.title: Fiscal and monetary policy
items.body: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxation, decided by the government and parliament. Monetary policy is control of interest rates and money supply, usually by the central bank. Both are used to steady the economy.

items.title: What is deflation?
items.body: Deflation is a general fall in prices. It sounds good, but it can be harmful: people delay purchases expecting lower prices, businesses earn less, and debts become harder to repay.

items.title: The euro
items.body: The euro was introduced as an electronic currency on 1 January 1999. Euro banknotes and coins entered circulation on 1 January 2002, replacing currencies such as the German mark and French franc.

items.title: Africa's free trade area
items.body: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) began trading on 1 January 2021. It aims to create a single market for goods and services across Africa by gradually removing tariffs between member states.
items.source_name: Wikipedia: African Continental Free Trade Area

items.title: The informal economy
items.body: The informal economy is economic activity that is not taxed or regulated by government, such as many street traders and small unregistered businesses. In many developing countries it employs most workers.

items.title: Government debt
items.body: Government debt is the total a government owes from past borrowing. It is often compared with GDP (debt-to-GDP ratio) to judge how affordable it is. Interest on debt competes with spending on schools and hospitals.

items.title: Externalities
items.body: An externality is a cost or benefit that affects people outside a transaction. Pollution from a factory is a negative externality; a neighbour's beautiful garden is a positive one. Taxes and rules are used to correct them.

items.title: Economics word: stagflation
items.body: Meaning: high inflation combined with slow growth and high unemployment at the same time.
items.example_sentence: The oil shocks of the 1970s caused stagflation in many countries.

items.title: Economics word: austerity
items.body: Meaning: government policies that cut spending or raise taxes to reduce a budget deficit.
items.example_sentence: The austerity budget cut funding for public projects.

items.title: Economics word: subsidy
items.body: Meaning: money given by government to lower the cost of a product or support an industry.
items.example_sentence: A fuel subsidy keeps petrol prices lower than their market level.

items.title: Economics word: commodity
items.body: Meaning: a basic good that is traded and largely the same whoever produces it, such as oil, copper, coffee or maize.
items.example_sentence: Copper is Zambia's most important export commodity.

items.title: Economics word: productivity
items.body: Meaning: how much output is produced per worker or per hour of work.
items.example_sentence: New machines raised the factory's productivity by 20%.

items.title: Economics word: liquidity
items.body: Meaning: how quickly and easily an asset can be turned into cash without losing value.
items.example_sentence: Cash has perfect liquidity; a house has very little.

items.title: Rising prices
items.body: Definitions check.
items.statement: Inflation means prices in general are rising
items.explanation: Inflation is a general, sustained rise in prices, so money buys less over time.

items.title: Demand goes up
items.body: Supply and demand.
items.statement: If demand rises and supply stays the same, prices usually fall
items.explanation: More buyers chasing the same amount of goods pushes prices up.

items.title: Measuring an economy
items.body: Definitions check.
items.statement: GDP measures the value of goods and services a country produces in a period
items.explanation: GDP is the total market value of final goods and services produced in a country in a given period.

items.title: Taxing imports
items.body: Trade check.
items.statement: A tariff is a tax on imported goods
items.explanation: Tariffs are taxes on imports, which raise their price in the local market.

items.title: Printing money
items.body: Money check.
items.statement: Printing lots of new money always makes a country richer
items.explanation: More money chasing the same goods raises prices. Zimbabwe in 2008 is an extreme example.

items.title: Trade deficit
items.body: Trade check.
items.statement: A trade deficit means a country imports more than it exports
items.explanation: Exports minus imports is negative when imports are larger. That gap is the trade deficit.

items.title: What deflation means
items.body: Definitions check.
items.statement: Deflation means prices are rising quickly
items.explanation: Deflation is a general fall in prices. Fast rising prices are high inflation.

items.title: The cost of a choice
items.body: Key concept.
items.statement: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up
items.explanation: Choosing one thing means not choosing another. The best option you gave up is the opportunity cost.

items.title: Fighting inflation
items.body: Central banks.
items.statement: Central banks often raise interest rates to fight high inflation
items.explanation: Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, which cools spending and slows price rises.

items.title: Euro cash
items.body: History check.
items.statement: Euro banknotes and coins entered circulation in 2002
items.explanation: The euro existed electronically from 1999; notes and coins arrived on 1 January 2002.

items.title: Word: meticulous
items.body: Meaning: showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise.
items.example_sentence: She kept meticulous records of every test.

items.title: Word: ubiquitous
items.body: Meaning: present, appearing or found everywhere.
items.example_sentence: Mobile phones have become ubiquitous in every city.

items.title: Word: pragmatic
items.body: Meaning: dealing with things in a practical, realistic way rather than by theory.
items.example_sentence: We need a pragmatic solution we can start this week.

items.title: Word: ambiguous
items.body: Meaning: open to more than one interpretation; not clear.
items.example_sentence: The contract's wording was ambiguous, so both sides disagreed.

items.title: Word: eloquent
items.body: Meaning: fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing.
items.example_sentence: Her eloquent speech moved the whole audience.

items.title: Word: resilient
items.body: Meaning: able to recover quickly from difficulties.
items.example_sentence: Small businesses proved resilient during the crisis.

items.title: Word: candid
items.body: Meaning: truthful and straightforward; frank.
items.example_sentence: Thank you for your candid feedback on my report.

items.title: Word: succinct
items.body: Meaning: briefly and clearly expressed.
items.example_sentence: Keep your answer succinct: two sentences at most.

items.title: Word: scrutinise
items.body: Meaning: to examine or inspect closely and thoroughly. Also spelled 'scrutinize'.
items.example_sentence: The committee will scrutinise the budget line by line.

items.title: Word: mitigate
items.body: Meaning: to make something bad less severe or serious.
items.example_sentence: Planting trees can help mitigate flooding.

items.title: Word: juxtapose
items.body: Meaning: to place two things side by side, especially to show a contrast.
items.example_sentence: The film juxtaposes wealth and poverty in the same street.

items.title: Word: ephemeral
items.body: Meaning: lasting for a very short time.
items.example_sentence: Social media fame is often ephemeral.

items.title: Word: diligent
items.body: Meaning: showing care and steady effort in your work.
items.example_sentence: A diligent student reviews notes every evening.

items.title: Word: conundrum
items.body: Meaning: a confusing and difficult problem or question.
items.example_sentence: Saving money while prices rise is a real conundrum.

items.title: Word: pertinent
items.body: Meaning: relevant to the matter being discussed.
items.example_sentence: Please keep your questions pertinent to today's topic.

items.title: Word: tenacious
items.body: Meaning: holding firmly to a goal; determined and persistent.
items.example_sentence: Her tenacious effort finally got the project funded.

items.title: Word: nuance
items.body: Meaning: a subtle difference in meaning, expression or sound.
items.example_sentence: A good translator understands the nuance of each word.

items.title: Phrase: in light of
items.body: Meaning: considering or because of something. Useful in formal writing.
items.example_sentence: In light of the new evidence, we changed our plan.

items.title: Phrase: by the same token
items.body: Meaning: for the same reason; in the same way. Use it to extend an argument.
items.example_sentence: Hard work brings rewards; by the same token, laziness has costs.

items.title: Phrase: it stands to reason
items.body: Meaning: it is logical or obvious.
items.example_sentence: If you practise daily, it stands to reason that you will improve.

items.title: Phrase: on balance
items.body: Meaning: after considering all the facts. A strong way to begin a conclusion.
items.example_sentence: On balance, the benefits of the plan outweigh the costs.

items.title: Phrase: a case in point
items.body: Meaning: a good example of what has just been said.
items.example_sentence: Some cities have cut traffic; Kigali's car-free days are a case in point.

items.title: Phrase: having said that
items.body: Meaning: despite what I have just said. Introduces a contrast politely.
items.example_sentence: The hotel was expensive. Having said that, the service was excellent.

items.title: Phrase: food for thought
items.body: Meaning: something worth thinking about seriously.
items.example_sentence: Your comments gave me a lot of food for thought.

items.title: Phrase: to put it another way
items.body: Meaning: said differently, to make something clearer.
items.example_sentence: We spend more than we earn. To put it another way, we are in debt.

items.title: What is a comma splice?
items.body: A comma splice joins two full sentences with only a comma. Wrong: 'I love tech, I love building.' Right: 'I love tech. I love building.' Or: 'I love tech, and I love building.' Or use a semicolon.

items.title: Its or it's?
items.body: 'It's' always means 'it is' or 'it has'. 'Its' shows ownership, with no apostrophe: 'The company changed its logo.' Test: if you can say 'it is', write 'it's'.

items.title: There, their, they're
items.body: 'There' is a place (over there). 'Their' shows ownership (their car). 'They're' means 'they are' (they're late). Read your sentence with 'they are' to test the third.

items.title: Fewer or less?
items.body: Use 'fewer' for things you can count: fewer cars, fewer mistakes. Use 'less' for things you measure: less water, less time. 'Fewer than 10 items', not 'less than 10 items'.

items.title: Affect or effect?
items.body: 'Affect' is usually a verb: 'Rain affects traffic.' 'Effect' is usually a noun: 'Rain has an effect on traffic.' Memory trick: Affect is the Action, Effect is the End result.

items.title: Subject-verb agreement
items.body: The verb must match the real subject, not the nearest noun. 'The list of items is long' (the list is long), not 'are long'. 'Each of the students has a book', not 'have'.

items.title: Parts of speech: adverbs
items.body: An adverb describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb. It often ends in -ly: 'She spoke clearly.' Some do not: fast, well, very, often. 'He runs fast' uses 'fast' as an adverb.

items.title: Active and passive voice
items.body: Active: the doer comes first. 'The manager approved the plan.' Passive: 'The plan was approved by the manager.' Active is usually clearer and shorter. Use passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

items.title: Who or whom?
items.body: 'Who' does the action (like he). 'Whom' receives it (like him). Test with he/him: 'Who called?' (he called). 'To whom did you write?' (you wrote to him).

items.title: i.e. or e.g.?
items.body: 'e.g.' means 'for example' (exempli gratia) and gives one or more examples. 'i.e.' means 'that is' (id est) and restates or clarifies. 'Bring fruit, e.g. apples' vs 'the capital, i.e. Nairobi'.

items.title: Their or they're?
items.body: Spot the error.
items.statement: 'Their going home now' is correct English
items.explanation: 'They're' means 'they are'. 'Their' shows ownership, as in 'their home'.

items.title: Fewer people
items.body: Countable or not?
items.statement: 'Fewer people came than expected' is correct
items.explanation: People can be counted, so 'fewer' is right. 'Less' is for amounts you measure.

items.title: Irregardless
items.body: Formal English check.
items.statement: 'Irregardless' is standard formal English
items.explanation: Dictionaries list 'irregardless' as nonstandard. In formal writing, use 'regardless'.

items.title: Spot the adverb
items.body: Parts of speech.
items.statement: In 'She sings beautifully', 'beautifully' is an adverb
items.explanation: 'Beautifully' describes how she sings, which is the verb, so it is an adverb.

items.title: Could of
items.body: Common mistake.
items.statement: 'I could of helped' is correct in formal writing
items.explanation: 'Could've' sounds like 'could of', but the correct form is 'could have'.

items.title: Between you and me
items.body: Pronoun check.
items.statement: 'Between you and I' is grammatically correct
items.explanation: After a preposition like 'between', use the object form: 'me', not 'I'.

items.title: Plural of criterion
items.body: Tricky plurals.
items.statement: The plural of 'criterion' is 'criteria'
items.explanation: 'Criterion' comes from Greek. One criterion, two criteria. Like phenomenon and phenomena.

items.title: Affect or effect in use
items.body: Word choice.
items.statement: 'The new law will effect everyone' uses the right word
items.correct_answer: The new law will affect everyone
items.explanation: Here we need the verb meaning 'to influence', which is 'affect'. 'Effect' is usually the noun.

items.title: Compound interest
items.body: With compound interest you earn interest on your savings and on the interest already added. Over many years this snowballs: money growing at 8% a year roughly doubles in 9 years and quadruples in 18.

items.title: Simple vs compound interest
items.body: Put 1,000 away at 10% a year for 2 years. Simple interest pays 100 each year: 1,200. Compound interest pays 100 in year one, then 10% of 1,100 (110) in year two: 1,210. The gap grows every year.

items.title: The rule of 72
items.body: To estimate how many years money takes to double, divide 72 by the yearly growth rate. At 6%, 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. It also works for debt and inflation: at 12% inflation, prices double in about 6 years.

items.title: Diversification
items.body: Diversification means spreading money across different investments, such as different companies, sectors and types of asset, so one failure does not wipe you out. It reduces risk without necessarily reducing returns.

items.title: Inflation eats cash
items.body: If inflation is 8% and your savings earn 3%, your money buys about 5% less each year even though the number grows. What matters is the real return: your interest rate minus inflation.

items.title: Stocks and bonds
items.body: A stock (share) is a small piece of ownership in a company; its value rises and falls with the company. A bond is a loan you make to a company or government, which pays you interest and returns your money at the end.

items.title: Index funds
items.body: An index fund owns all the shares in a market index, such as the 500 companies in the S&P 500, instead of trying to pick winners. It offers wide diversification and usually low fees.

items.title: What APR tells you
items.body: The annual percentage rate (APR) shows the yearly cost of a loan, including interest and many fees, as a single percentage. Comparing APRs is a better way to compare loans than looking at monthly payments.

items.title: Credit scores
items.body: A credit score is a number lenders use to judge how likely you are to repay debt. Paying bills on time and not borrowing close to your limits tend to improve it. A better score usually means cheaper loans.

items.title: Your net worth
items.body: Net worth = what you own (assets) minus what you owe (liabilities). A house worth 50,000 with a 30,000 loan left adds 20,000 to your net worth. Tracking it once a year shows real progress.

items.title: Revenue is not profit
items.body: Revenue is all the money a business takes in from sales. Profit is what is left after paying all costs: stock, rent, wages, taxes and interest. A business can have high revenue and still make a loss.

items.title: Cash flow
items.body: Cash flow is the money moving in and out of a business or household over time. A profitable business can still fail if customers pay late and it cannot cover bills today. Watch the timing, not just the totals.

items.title: Dollar-cost averaging
items.body: Investing a fixed amount at regular times, for example every month, whatever the price. You automatically buy more when prices are low and less when they are high, and you avoid trying to time the market.

items.title: Risk and return
items.body: Investments that can earn more usually carry more risk of loss. Savings accounts are safe but grow slowly; shares can grow faster but can fall sharply. Be suspicious of anyone promising high returns with no risk.

items.title: How Ponzi schemes work
items.body: A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors with money from new investors instead of real profits. It needs ever more new money, so it always collapses. Warning signs: guaranteed high returns and pressure to recruit others.

items.title: M-Pesa
items.body: M-Pesa, launched in Kenya in 2007 by Safaricom and Vodafone, lets people send, receive and store money using a basic mobile phone. It brought financial services to millions of people without bank accounts.

items.title: Dividends
items.body: A dividend is a share of a company's profit paid out to its shareholders, often every quarter or year. Not all companies pay them; some reinvest profits to grow instead.

items.title: The break-even point
items.body: Break-even is the level of sales where total income equals total costs, so there is no profit and no loss. Fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit) gives the number of units you must sell.

items.title: What collateral is
items.body: Collateral is an asset a borrower pledges to secure a loan, such as a house, car or land. If the loan is not repaid, the lender can take the collateral. Secured loans usually have lower interest rates.

items.title: Budgeting basics
items.body: A budget plans where your money goes before you spend it. List your income, then fixed costs (rent, transport), then savings, then flexible spending. Saving first, as soon as you are paid, makes it far more likely to happen.

items.title: Emergency savings
items.body: An emergency fund is money kept aside for surprises such as job loss or medical bills. A common guideline is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach.

items.title: Good debt and bad debt
items.body: Borrowing to buy something that grows in value or raises your income, such as training or equipment for a business, can make sense. Borrowing at high interest for things that lose value quickly usually does not.

items.title: What an asset is
items.body: An asset is anything you own that has value or produces income: cash, land, a business, shares. A liability is something you owe: loans and unpaid bills. Building wealth means growing assets faster than liabilities.

items.title: Fees add up
items.body: A 2% yearly fee sounds small, but over 30 years it can take a large share of your investment growth, because the fee is charged on your whole balance every year. Always check the costs of any investment.

items.title: Finance word: equity
items.body: Meaning: ownership value, such as shares in a company, or the part of a house you own outright after the loan.
items.example_sentence: After ten years of payments, she had built up equity in her home.

items.title: Finance word: portfolio
items.body: Meaning: the collection of all the investments a person or organisation holds.
items.example_sentence: His portfolio includes shares, bonds and some land.

items.title: Finance word: overhead
items.body: Meaning: the ongoing costs of running a business that are not tied to a specific product, such as rent and electricity.
items.example_sentence: Working from home kept the startup's overhead low.

items.title: Finance word: principal
items.body: Meaning: the original amount of money borrowed or invested, not counting interest.
items.example_sentence: Each payment covers some interest and some of the principal.

items.title: Finance word: yield
items.body: Meaning: the income an investment produces, usually shown as a yearly percentage of its price.
items.example_sentence: The bond has a yield of 7% a year.

items.title: Finance word: default
items.body: Meaning: failing to repay a debt on time as agreed.
items.example_sentence: Missing three payments put the loan in default.

items.title: Interest on interest
items.body: Saving check.
items.statement: With compound interest you also earn interest on past interest
items.explanation: Interest is added to your balance and then earns interest itself. That is compounding.

items.title: Doubling money
items.body: Rule of 72.
items.statement: By the rule of 72, money growing at 6% a year doubles in about 12 years
items.explanation: 72 ÷ 6 = 12. The exact answer is about 11.9 years.

items.title: Simple interest
items.body: Interest check.
items.statement: 1,000 at 10% simple interest for 2 years grows to 1,210
items.explanation: Simple interest pays 10% of the original 1,000 each year: 100 + 100 = 200. 1,210 is the compound result.

items.title: Revenue and profit
items.body: Business check.
items.statement: Revenue and profit mean the same thing
items.correct_answer: No: profit is revenue minus costs
items.explanation: Revenue is all money from sales. Profit is what remains after paying every cost.

items.title: Spreading risk
items.body: Investing check.
items.statement: Diversifying means spreading money across different investments
items.explanation: Spreading money means one bad investment cannot sink everything.

items.title: Spot the scam
items.body: Fraud check.
items.statement: A Ponzi scheme pays old investors with money from new investors
items.explanation: There are no real profits, only new money moving to older investors, so it must collapse.

items.title: Measuring wealth
items.body: Personal finance check.
items.statement: Net worth is what you own minus what you owe
items.explanation: Assets minus liabilities equals net worth.

items.title: Cash and inflation
items.body: Saving check.
items.statement: Keeping all your savings in cash fully protects them from inflation
items.correct_answer: Inflation reduces what cash can buy
items.explanation: Cash keeps its number but loses buying power when prices rise.

items.title: What a bond is
items.body: Investing check.
items.statement: Buying a bond means lending money to a company or government
items.explanation: A bond is a loan. The issuer pays interest and returns the money at maturity.

items.title: Mobile money origins
items.body: Fintech check.
items.statement: M-Pesa mobile money was launched in Kenya
items.explanation: Safaricom and Vodafone launched M-Pesa in Kenya in 2007.

items.title: Asking how someone is
items.body: A polite everyday greeting.
items.example_sentence: Bonjour madame, comment allez-vous ?

items.title: Saying hello
items.body: The standard greeting all day until evening. Say it when you enter a shop. Sounds like 'bon-ZHOOR'.
items.example_sentence: Bonjour, je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.

items.title: A casual 'how are you?'
items.body: Informal, for friends and family. The answer can be the same words: 'Ça va !' (I'm fine!).
items.example_sentence: Salut Paul, ça va ?

items.title: Nice to meet you
items.body: Said when meeting someone. Written 'enchantée' by a woman; it sounds the same. Sounds like 'on-shon-TAY'.
items.example_sentence: Je m'appelle Awa. Enchantée !

items.title: Saying please
items.body: The polite form. With friends you can say 's'il te plaît'.
items.example_sentence: L'addition, s'il vous plaît.

items.title: Thank you very much
items.body: The 'r' in merci is soft, from the throat. Reply to thanks with 'de rien' (you're welcome).
items.example_sentence: Merci beaucoup pour votre aide.

items.title: When you don't understand
items.body: Very useful for learners. 'Ne' is often dropped in speech: 'Je comprends pas'.
items.example_sentence: Pardon, je ne comprends pas.

items.title: Asking someone to repeat
items.body: Polite and useful. You can add 'plus lentement' (more slowly).
items.example_sentence: Pouvez-vous répéter plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ?

items.title: Finding the toilets
items.body: Always plural in French: 'les toilettes'.
items.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, où sont les toilettes ?

items.title: Asking the price
items.body: Essential at the market.
items.example_sentence: Ce sac, combien ça coûte ?

items.title: Ordering politely
items.body: 'Je voudrais' (I would like) is more polite than 'je veux' (I want).
items.term: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît
items.translation: I would like a coffee, please
items.example_sentence: Je voudrais un café et un croissant, s'il vous plaît.

items.title: Getting attention
items.body: Use it to stop someone politely or to say sorry for a small thing.
items.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, la gare est loin ?

items.title: Introducing yourself
items.body: Literally 'I call myself'.
items.example_sentence: Bonjour, je m'appelle Thomas.

items.title: See you soon
items.body: A friendly goodbye when you expect to meet again.
items.example_sentence: Merci pour tout, à bientôt !

items.title: Have a good day
items.body: Said when leaving a shop or ending a call. In the evening say 'bonne soirée'.
items.example_sentence: Merci monsieur, bonne journée !

items.title: Agreeing
items.body: Very common in conversation. Sounds like 'dah-KOR'.
items.example_sentence: On se voit à midi ? D'accord.

items.title: Asking the time
items.body: The answer starts with 'Il est...': 'Il est trois heures' (It is three o'clock).
items.example_sentence: Pardon, quelle heure est-il ?

items.title: Saying sorry
items.body: Written 'désolée' by a woman. For a small bump, 'pardon' is enough.
items.example_sentence: Je suis désolé, je suis en retard.

items.title: Asking about English
items.body: Useful when you are stuck.
items.example_sentence: Excusez-moi, parlez-vous anglais ?

items.title: Enjoy your meal
items.body: Said before eating. English borrowed the phrase too.
items.example_sentence: Le dîner est prêt. Bon appétit !

items.title: Word: le travail
items.body: Masculine noun. The verb is 'travailler' (to work).
items.example_sentence: Je vais au travail en bus.

items.title: Word: la maison
items.body: Feminine noun. 'À la maison' means at home.
items.example_sentence: Je reste à la maison ce soir.

items.title: Word: l'eau
items.body: Feminine noun. Sounds like 'LOH'. Tap water: 'l'eau du robinet'.
items.example_sentence: Une bouteille d'eau, s'il vous plaît.

items.title: Word: aujourd'hui
items.body: One of the most useful time words. Sounds like 'oh-zhoor-DWEE'.
items.example_sentence: Aujourd'hui, il fait beau.

items.title: Word: demain
items.body: Pairs with 'hier' (yesterday) and 'aujourd'hui' (today).
items.example_sentence: À demain !

items.title: Word: hier
items.body: Sounds like 'ee-YAIR'.
items.example_sentence: Hier, j'ai visité le musée.

items.title: Word: la gare
items.body: Feminine noun. A bus station is 'la gare routière'.
items.example_sentence: La gare est à dix minutes à pied.

items.title: Word: l'argent
items.body: Masculine noun. It also means the metal silver.
items.example_sentence: Je n'ai pas assez d'argent.

items.title: Word: le marché
items.body: Masculine noun. 'Faire le marché' means to do the market shopping.
items.example_sentence: Le marché ouvre à sept heures.

items.title: Tu or vous?
items.body: 'Tu' is informal 'you' for friends, family and children. 'Vous' is polite 'you' for strangers, older people and at work, and also plural 'you'. When unsure, use 'vous'.

items.title: Every noun has a gender
items.body: French nouns are masculine (le) or feminine (la). Before a vowel both become l'. Plural is always les. Learn each noun with its article: le livre (book), la table (table).

items.title: Silent final letters
items.body: Final consonants are usually silent: 'petit' sounds like 'puh-TEE', 'Paris' like 'pah-REE'. Often the letters c, r, f and l are pronounced at the end, as in 'avec', 'bonjour', 'neuf', 'mal'.

items.title: Linking words: liaison
items.body: A silent final consonant is often pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel. 'Les amis' sounds like 'lay-za-MEE', and 'vous avez' like 'voo-za-VAY'.

items.title: Making a sentence negative
items.body: Wrap the verb with 'ne ... pas'. 'Je parle' (I speak) becomes 'Je ne parle pas' (I don't speak). Before a vowel, 'ne' becomes 'n'': 'Je n'aime pas'.

items.title: Counting from 70 to 99
items.body: French counts 70 as 'sixty-ten' (soixante-dix), 80 as 'four-twenties' (quatre-vingts) and 90 as 'four-twenty-ten' (quatre-vingt-dix). In Belgium and Switzerland, 70 is 'septante' and 90 is 'nonante'.

items.title: Please or thanks?
items.body: Everyday French.
items.statement: 'Merci' means 'please' in French
items.explanation: 'Merci' means thank you. 'Please' is 's'il vous plaît' (formal) or 's'il te plaît' (informal).

items.title: The book
items.body: Basic vocabulary.
items.statement: 'Le livre' means 'the book'
items.explanation: 'Le livre' is the book. Careful: 'la livre' means a pound (weight or money).

items.title: Polite 'you'
items.body: Tu or vous?
items.statement: 'Vous' is used for the polite or formal 'you'
items.explanation: 'Vous' is polite and also plural. 'Tu' is for people you know well.

items.title: French numbers
items.body: Counting check.
items.statement: In French, 'soixante-dix' means 60
items.explanation: 'Soixante' is 60 and 'dix' is 10, so 'soixante-dix' (sixty-ten) is 70.

items.title: Evening greeting
items.body: Greetings check.
items.statement: 'Bonsoir' means 'good evening'
items.explanation: Use 'bonsoir' from late afternoon. 'Bonne nuit' (good night) is only for going to bed.

items.title: Cat or dog?
items.body: Animal words.
items.statement: 'Chat' in French means 'dog'
items.explanation: 'Le chat' is the cat and 'le chien' is the dog.

items.title: Saying goodbye
items.body: Everyday French.
items.statement: 'Au revoir' means 'goodbye'
items.explanation: 'Au revoir' literally means 'until we see again'.

items.title: Quick multiplication
items.body: Multiplication check.
items.explanation: 7 × 7 = 49. A quick check: 7 × 5 = 35, plus 7 × 2 = 14, gives 49.

items.title: A dozen dozens
items.body: Squares you should know by heart.
items.explanation: 12 × 12 = 144, also called a gross. Check: 12 × 10 = 120, plus 12 × 2 = 24, gives 144.

items.title: Percent of a number
items.body: Mental percentages.

items.title: A quarter of 80
items.body: Mental percentages.
items.explanation: 25% is one quarter. 80 ÷ 4 = 20.

items.title: Times table check
items.body: Multiplication check.

items.title: Six sevens
items.body: Multiplication check.

items.title: Multiplying decimals
items.body: Half of a half.
items.explanation: Half of a half is a quarter: 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25.

items.title: Adding fractions
items.body: Fractions check.
items.explanation: Add the tops when the bottoms match: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2. The bottom number does not change.

items.title: Square roots
items.body: Square root check.
items.statement: The square root of 81 is 9
items.explanation: 9 × 9 = 81, so the square root of 81 is 9.

items.title: Powers of two
items.body: Powers check.
items.statement: 2 to the power of 10 is 1,024

items.title: Is it prime?
items.body: Prime number check.
items.statement: 17 is a prime number
items.explanation: 17 can only be divided exactly by 1 and 17, so it is prime.

items.title: A tricky prime
items.body: Prime number check.
items.statement: 51 is a prime number
items.explanation: 5 + 1 = 6, which divides by 3, so 51 divides by 3: 51 = 3 × 17.

items.title: Solve for x
items.body: Basic algebra.
items.statement: If 3x + 5 = 20, then x = 5
items.explanation: Subtract 5 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.

items.title: Solve for x again
items.body: Basic algebra.
items.statement: If 2x − 4 = 10, then x = 3
items.explanation: Add 4 to both sides: 2x = 14. Divide by 2: x = 7.

items.title: Up 10%, down 10%
items.body: Percentage change trap.
items.statement: A 10% rise then a 10% fall brings a price back to where it started
items.explanation: 100 up 10% is 110. 110 down 10% is 110 − 11 = 99. The fall is taken from a bigger number.

items.title: Triangle angles
items.body: Geometry check.
items.statement: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°
items.explanation: In any flat triangle the three inside angles always add up to 180°.

items.title: Times eleven
items.body: Multiplication check.
items.explanation: Put the sum of the digits in the middle: 1, (1 + 3), 3 gives 143.

items.title: Dividing by a half
items.body: Division trap.
items.explanation: Dividing by 0.5 means asking how many halves fit in 45. That is 90. Dividing by a half doubles a number.

items.title: Fraction to decimal
items.body: Fractions and decimals.

items.title: Finding the average
items.body: Mean check.
items.statement: The average of 4, 8 and 12 is 8
items.explanation: Add them: 4 + 8 + 12 = 24. Divide by how many there are: 24 ÷ 3 = 8.

items.title: Negative times negative
items.body: Signs check.
items.explanation: A negative times a negative is positive: (−3) × (−4) = 12.

items.title: Area of a square
items.body: Geometry check.
items.statement: A square with 5 cm sides has an area of 20 cm²
items.explanation: Area = side × side = 5 × 5 = 25 cm². 20 cm is its perimeter (4 × 5), not its area.

items.title: Swapping percentages
items.body: Percent trick.
items.statement: 20% of 50 equals 50% of 20
items.explanation: x% of y always equals y% of x. Here both are 10.

items.title: Dividing by eight
items.body: Division check.
items.explanation: Halve three times: 1,000 → 500 → 250 → 125.

items.title: Near a hundred
items.body: Multiplication check.

items.title: Two answers
items.body: Algebra trap.
items.statement: x² = 49 has only one solution, x = 7
items.explanation: (−7) × (−7) is also 49, so there are two solutions: 7 and −7.

items.title: Order of operations
items.body: Brackets, powers, times and divide, plus and minus.
items.explanation: Multiply before adding: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14. You only get 20 with brackets: (2 + 3) × 4.

items.title: Multiply by 11 in your head
items.body: For a two-digit number, write its digits apart and put their sum in the middle. 34 × 11: 3, (3 + 4 = 7), 4 gives 374. If the sum is 10 or more, carry 1 to the left: 57 × 11 is 5, 12, 7, so 627.

items.title: The percentage swap trick
items.body: x% of y equals y% of x. Hard ones become easy: 8% of 25 is the same as 25% of 8, which is 2. And 4% of 75 is 75% of 4, which is 3.

items.title: Squaring numbers ending in 5
items.body: Take the first digit, multiply it by the next number up, then write 25 after it. 35²: 3 × 4 = 12, so 1,225. 65²: 6 × 7 = 42, so 4,225.

items.title: Multiply by 5 quickly
items.body: Multiplying by 5 is the same as multiplying by 10 and halving. 5 × 68: 680 ÷ 2 = 340. 5 × 43: 430 ÷ 2 = 215.

items.title: What is a prime number?
items.body: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that can only be divided exactly by 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13... The number 2 is the only even prime. 1 is not prime.

items.title: The order of operations
items.body: Work in this order: Brackets, then powers, then multiply and divide from left to right, then add and subtract from left to right. So 10 − 2 × 3 = 10 − 6 = 4, not 24.

items.title: Solving a simple equation
items.body: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other, until x is alone. 4x + 3 = 23: take 3 from both sides (4x = 20), then divide both sides by 4 (x = 5). Check: 4 × 5 + 3 = 23.

items.title: Working out a percentage change
items.body: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. A price going from 80 to 100: (100 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100 = 25% rise. Always divide by the starting value.

items.title: Divisible by 3 or 9?
items.body: Add the digits. If the sum divides by 3, the number divides by 3. If the sum divides by 9, the number divides by 9. 2,457: 2 + 4 + 5 + 7 = 18, so it divides by both 3 and 9.

items.title: Mean, median and mode
items.body: Mean: add everything and divide by the count. Median: the middle value when sorted. Mode: the most common value. For 2, 3, 3, 8, 14: mean 6, median 3, mode 3. One big value pulls the mean but not the median.

items.title: Estimate before you calculate
items.body: Round first to see the rough answer: 49 × 21 is about 50 × 20 = 1,000. The exact answer (1,029) should be close. If your calculation gives 10,290, you know something went wrong.

items.title: Logic: the Monty Hall puzzle
items.body: A prize is behind one of 3 doors. You pick one. The host, who knows, opens another door with no prize and lets you switch. Switching wins 2 times in 3, because your first pick was right only 1 time in 3.

items.title: Zero as a number
items.body: The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with zero, including adding and subtracting it, in 628 CE. Treating zero as a number in its own right was a huge step for mathematics.

items.title: Pi never ends
items.body: Pi (π), the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, is about 3.14159. It is irrational: its decimals go on forever without repeating, so it can never be written exactly as a fraction.

items.title: The birthday paradox
items.body: In a room of just 23 people, there is a better than 50% chance that two of them share a birthday. It feels wrong, but there are 253 different pairs of people to compare.

items.title: What is a googol?
items.body: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros (10¹⁰⁰). The name was coined by a young boy, the nephew of mathematician Edward Kasner, in the 1920s. The company name Google was inspired by it.

items.title: Separation of powers
items.body: Many constitutions split government into three branches: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets them. The idea, linked to the French thinker Montesquieu, is that each branch checks the others.

items.title: Where 'democracy' comes from
items.body: The word democracy comes from the Greek 'demos' (people) and 'kratos' (power or rule): rule by the people. Ancient Athens practised an early direct form of it in the 5th century BCE.

items.title: Parliamentary systems
items.body: In a parliamentary system the head of government (usually a prime minister) comes from and depends on the support of parliament. If parliament loses confidence in the government, it can be removed. Examples include the UK, India and Japan.

items.title: Presidential systems
items.body: In a presidential system the president is both head of state and head of government, is elected separately from the legislature, and serves a fixed term. Examples include the United States, Brazil and Kenya.

items.title: What is federalism?
items.body: In a federal system, power is shared between a national government and regional governments such as states or provinces, each with its own powers set by the constitution. Examples: the United States, Nigeria, India and Germany.

items.title: What is a unitary state?
items.body: In a unitary state the central government holds most power. Local governments exist, but their powers are given, and can be changed, by the centre. France and Japan are examples.

items.title: What a constitution does
items.body: A constitution is the supreme law of a country. It sets out how government is organised, what powers each part has, and often the rights of citizens. Other laws must not contradict it.

items.title: Magna Carta, 1215
items.body: In 1215 King John of England agreed to Magna Carta, a charter limiting royal power. Its principle that even the ruler is subject to the law influenced later constitutions around the world.

items.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
items.body: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948. It sets out 30 articles of basic rights. 10 December is now Human Rights Day.
items.source_name: United Nations: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

items.title: First past the post
items.body: Under 'first past the post', each area elects one representative: whoever gets the most votes wins, even without a majority. It is simple, but a party's share of seats can differ a lot from its share of votes.

items.title: Proportional representation
items.body: In proportional representation, parties win seats roughly in line with their share of the vote. 30% of votes gives about 30% of seats. It often leads to coalition governments. South Africa and the Netherlands use forms of it.

items.title: What is a referendum?
items.body: A referendum is a direct vote in which all voters decide on a single question, such as a new constitution or leaving an organisation, instead of leaving the decision to elected representatives.

items.title: Constitutional monarchy
items.body: In a constitutional monarchy, a king or queen is head of state but their powers are limited by a constitution, and elected politicians run the government. Examples: the UK, Japan and Lesotho. In an absolute monarchy, the monarch holds full power.

items.title: Two chambers
items.body: A bicameral legislature has two chambers, such as a lower house and an upper house or senate. Laws usually need approval from both. A unicameral legislature has only one chamber.

items.title: The rule of law
items.body: The rule of law means everyone, including government leaders, is subject to laws that are public, applied equally and decided by independent courts, rather than to the arbitrary will of those in power.

items.title: South Africa's 1994 election
items.body: South Africa's first election in which all races could vote was held in April 1994. Nelson Mandela became the country's first democratically elected president in May 1994.

items.title: The Berlin Wall falls
items.body: The Berlin Wall, which divided East and West Berlin from 1961, was opened on 9 November 1989. Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990.

items.title: Women's right to vote
items.body: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give all women the right to vote in national elections.
items.source_name: Wikipedia: Women's suffrage in New Zealand

items.title: What is impeachment?
items.body: Impeachment is a process in which a legislature formally charges a senior official, such as a president, with serious misconduct. Depending on the country, a conviction can lead to removal from office.

items.title: Coalition governments
items.body: When no single party wins a majority, two or more parties may agree to govern together as a coalition, sharing ministries and agreeing a common programme.

items.title: Judicial review
items.body: Judicial review is the power of courts to check whether laws or government actions follow the constitution, and to strike them down if they do not.

items.title: Head of state vs head of government
items.body: The head of state represents the country, often in a ceremonial role. The head of government runs the government day to day. In some countries one person does both; in others, like Germany, they are separate.

items.title: Why 'left' and 'right'?
items.body: The terms left and right in politics come from the French Revolution. In the National Assembly of 1789, supporters of the king sat on the right of the president and supporters of revolution on the left.

items.title: Term limits
items.body: A term limit restricts how many times, or how long, a person can hold an office. Many presidential systems limit presidents to two terms. Supporters see them as a check on power; critics say voters should decide.

items.title: Ghana's independence, 1957
items.body: Ghana, formerly the Gold Coast, gained independence from Britain on 6 March 1957, led by Kwame Nkrumah. It was among the first colonies in sub-Saharan Africa to become independent.

items.title: The role of the opposition
items.body: Parties not in government form the opposition. They question and scrutinise the government, propose alternative policies and offer voters a choice at the next election.

items.title: Politics word: sovereignty
items.body: Meaning: supreme authority of a state to govern itself without outside interference.
items.example_sentence: The treaty respects each country's sovereignty over its own borders.

items.title: Politics word: manifesto
items.body: Meaning: a public statement of a party's policies and aims, usually published before an election.
items.example_sentence: The party's manifesto promised free school meals.

items.title: Politics word: constituency
items.body: Meaning: an area whose voters elect a representative, and also the voters themselves.
items.example_sentence: She held regular meetings with people in her constituency.

items.title: Politics word: veto
items.body: Meaning: the power to reject a decision or law. From Latin for 'I forbid'.
items.example_sentence: The president used a veto to block the bill.

items.title: Politics word: incumbent
items.body: Meaning: the person who currently holds an office.
items.example_sentence: The incumbent mayor is running for a second term.

items.title: Politics word: electorate
items.body: Meaning: all the people entitled to vote in an election.
items.example_sentence: Young people make up a growing share of the electorate.

items.title: Where prime ministers come from
items.body: Systems of government.
items.statement: In a parliamentary system, the head of government usually comes from the legislature
items.explanation: The prime minister is usually a member of parliament and needs its support to stay in office.

items.title: Who makes laws?
items.body: Branches of government.
items.statement: The judiciary's main role is to make laws
items.explanation: The legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out and the judiciary interprets and applies them.

items.title: Magna Carta date
items.body: History check.
items.statement: Magna Carta was agreed in 1815
items.explanation: King John agreed to Magna Carta in 1215, six centuries earlier.

items.title: Direct democracy
items.body: Voting check.
items.statement: A referendum lets citizens vote directly on a specific question
items.explanation: In a referendum voters decide one question themselves instead of leaving it to representatives.

items.title: Human rights declaration
items.body: History check.
items.statement: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948
items.explanation: The UN General Assembly adopted it on 10 December 1948 in Paris.
items.source_name: United Nations: Universal Declaration of Human Rights

items.title: Federal power
items.body: Systems of government.
items.statement: In a federal system, all power belongs to the central government
items.explanation: Federal systems share power between national and regional governments. Central control describes a unitary state.

items.title: Mandela's presidency
items.body: History check.
items.statement: Nelson Mandela became president of South Africa in 1994
items.explanation: He was inaugurated in May 1994 after the country's first fully democratic election.

items.title: The Berlin Wall
items.body: History check.
items.statement: The Berlin Wall fell in 1991
items.explanation: The wall was opened on 9 November 1989. German reunification followed in 1990.

items.title: Counting chambers
items.body: Parliament check.
items.statement: A 'bicameral' parliament has two chambers
items.explanation: 'Bi' means two. A bicameral parliament has two houses, such as an assembly and a senate.

items.title: The birth of the United Nations
items.body: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945, now celebrated as United Nations Day. The UN replaced the League of Nations, created after World War I.

items.title: The UN Security Council
items.body: The Security Council has 15 members. Five are permanent and hold a veto: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The other ten are elected for two-year terms.

items.title: 193 member states
items.body: As of 2025, the United Nations has 193 member states. South Sudan, in 2011, was the most recent country to join. Two observer states, the Holy See and Palestine, are not full members.
items.source_name: Wikipedia: Member states of the United Nations

items.title: The African Union
items.body: The African Union (AU) was launched in 2002 in Durban, South Africa, replacing the Organisation of African Unity. It has 55 member states and its headquarters are in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

items.title: Africa Day
items.body: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was founded on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 independent African states. 25 May is celebrated as Africa Day.

items.title: SADC
items.body: The Southern African Development Community (SADC) promotes economic integration, peace and security in southern Africa. It was established in 1992, succeeding a coordination conference formed in 1980. Its headquarters are in Gaborone, Botswana.

items.title: ECOWAS
items.body: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was founded by the Treaty of Lagos on 28 May 1975 to promote economic integration in West Africa. Its headquarters are in Abuja, Nigeria.

items.title: The European Union
items.body: The European Union is a political and economic union of European countries. As of 2025 it has 27 member states, after the United Kingdom left in 2020. Most members use the euro as their currency.

items.title: NATO
items.body: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is a military alliance founded in 1949. Under Article 5 of its treaty, an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

items.title: Embassies and consulates
items.body: An embassy is a country's main diplomatic mission in a foreign capital, led by an ambassador. Consulates are smaller offices, often in other cities, that help citizens abroad and issue visas.

items.title: Diplomatic immunity
items.body: The 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations sets the rules for diplomacy, including diplomatic immunity: diplomats cannot be prosecuted by the host country, though they can be expelled.
items.source_name: Wikipedia: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations

items.title: The Peace of Westphalia
items.body: The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe. It is often seen as the origin of the modern idea of sovereign states that do not interfere in each other's internal affairs.

items.title: Bretton Woods, 1944
items.body: At the Bretton Woods conference in New Hampshire, USA, in July 1944, 44 Allied nations agreed a new international monetary system and created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

items.title: The World Trade Organization
items.body: The World Trade Organization (WTO) began on 1 January 1995, replacing the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947. It sets rules for trade between nations and settles trade disputes. It is based in Geneva.

items.title: BRICS
items.body: BRICS began as a grouping of Brazil, Russia, India and China; South Africa joined in 2010. The group expanded from 2024 with new members including Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

items.title: The Non-Aligned Movement
items.body: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in Belgrade in 1961 by countries that chose not to formally join either side in the Cold War. Leaders of India, Egypt, Yugoslavia, Ghana and Indonesia played key roles.

items.title: Hard power and soft power
items.body: Hard power is getting what you want through force or payment, like military action or sanctions. Soft power, a term coined by Joseph Nye, is attraction: culture, values and policies that make others want to cooperate.

items.title: The Commonwealth
items.body: The Commonwealth of Nations is a voluntary association of 56 member countries, as of 2025, most of them former British territories. Gabon and Togo, which have no historic ties to Britain, joined in 2022.

items.title: The International Court of Justice
items.body: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), in The Hague, Netherlands, is the UN's main court. It settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions. It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms.

items.title: The International Criminal Court
items.body: The International Criminal Court (ICC), which began work in 2002 in The Hague, tries individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression. Unlike the ICJ, it prosecutes people, not states.

items.title: Economic sanctions
items.body: Sanctions are penalties one or more countries place on another, such as trade bans, frozen assets or travel bans, to pressure a change in behaviour without using military force.

items.title: The Geneva Conventions
items.body: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 set rules for the humane treatment of wounded soldiers, prisoners of war and civilians during armed conflict. Every UN member state has ratified them.

items.title: The Paris Agreement
items.body: Adopted in December 2015, the Paris Agreement on climate change aims to keep global warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.

items.title: The UN General Assembly
items.body: The General Assembly is the UN body where all 193 member states meet, each with one vote regardless of size. Its resolutions are mostly recommendations; binding decisions on peace and security come from the Security Council.

items.title: Bilateral and multilateral
items.body: Bilateral relations are between two countries, such as a trade deal between Kenya and India. Multilateral relations involve three or more countries, often through organisations such as the UN, the AU or the WTO.

items.title: Word: ratify
items.body: Meaning: to formally approve a treaty so it becomes legally binding on a country, usually through parliament.
items.example_sentence: Parliament voted to ratify the trade agreement.

items.title: Word: embargo
items.body: Meaning: an official ban on trade or other activity with a particular country.
items.example_sentence: The arms embargo banned all weapons sales to the region.

items.title: Word: envoy
items.body: Meaning: a messenger or representative sent by a government on a special diplomatic mission.
items.example_sentence: The UN sent a special envoy to help with peace talks.

items.title: Word: détente
items.body: Meaning: the easing of tension between rival countries. Often used for the Cold War period of the 1970s.
items.example_sentence: The summit marked a new détente between the two neighbours.

items.title: Word: bloc
items.body: Meaning: a group of countries that act together because of shared interests.
items.example_sentence: The trade bloc negotiated as one with larger economies.

items.title: Veto powers
items.body: UN check.
items.statement: The UN Security Council has five permanent members with a veto
items.explanation: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US can each veto Security Council resolutions.

items.title: AU headquarters
items.body: Africa check.
items.statement: The African Union's headquarters is in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
items.explanation: The AU, like the OAU before it, is based in Addis Ababa.

items.title: SADC headquarters
items.body: Africa check.
items.statement: SADC's headquarters is in Nairobi, Kenya
items.explanation: SADC is based in Gaborone. Kenya is not a SADC member; it belongs to the East African Community.

items.title: When the UN began
items.body: History check.
items.statement: The United Nations was founded in 1919
items.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945 after World War II. The League of Nations came first, after World War I.

items.title: NATO's founding
items.body: History check.
items.statement: NATO was founded in 1949
items.explanation: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington in April 1949.

items.title: The World Court
items.body: International law check.
items.statement: The International Court of Justice is in The Hague
items.explanation: The ICJ sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague.

items.title: Why 25 May?
items.body: Africa check.
items.statement: Africa Day on 25 May marks the founding of the OAU in 1963
items.explanation: The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963.

items.title: From GATT to WTO
items.body: Trade check.
items.statement: The WTO replaced GATT in 1995
items.explanation: The WTO started on 1 January 1995 and took over the GATT rules.

items.title: Votes in the General Assembly
items.body: UN check.
items.statement: Every UN member state has one vote in the General Assembly
items.explanation: Each of the 193 members has one vote, whatever its size or wealth.

items.title: Bretton Woods
items.body: History check.
items.statement: The IMF and World Bank were created at the Bretton Woods conference in 1944
items.explanation: 44 Allied nations met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944 and created both institutions.

items.title: Sunlight is 8 minutes old
items.body: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth. When you look at the Sun, you see it as it was just over 8 minutes ago.

items.title: Boiling point and altitude
items.body: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level. Higher up, air pressure is lower, so water boils at a lower temperature. On top of Mount Everest it boils at roughly 70 °C, which is why cooking takes longer there.

items.title: 206 bones
items.body: An adult human skeleton usually has 206 bones. Babies are born with around 270, and many of them fuse together as the body grows.

items.title: The double helix
items.body: In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described DNA's double helix structure. Their model relied on X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling.

items.title: How photosynthesis works
items.body: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose (sugar) and oxygen. It happens mainly in the leaves, inside chloroplasts, using the green pigment chlorophyll. Almost all oxygen we breathe comes from it.

items.title: The speed of light
items.body: Light travels through a vacuum at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, about 300,000 km every second. Nothing carrying information can travel faster.

items.title: What causes tides
items.body: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans, with a smaller effect from the Sun. Most coasts get two high tides and two low tides a day.

items.title: The biggest planet
items.body: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. It is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined, and about 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.

items.title: The hottest planet
items.body: Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping the surface around 465 °C, hot enough to melt lead.

items.title: Antibiotics and viruses
items.body: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them growing. They do not work against viruses such as colds and flu. Using them when they are not needed helps bacteria become resistant.

items.title: The discovery of penicillin
items.body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould, Penicillium, killed bacteria growing in a dish in his London lab. Penicillin became the first widely used antibiotic in the 1940s.

items.title: Why blood is red
items.body: Red blood cells are full of haemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the body. The iron-based haem group gives blood its red colour.

items.title: The speed of sound
items.body: Sound travels through air at about 343 metres per second at 20 °C. It moves faster through water and even faster through solids like steel.

items.title: 118 elements
items.body: The periodic table has 118 confirmed chemical elements. The last four, including oganesson (element 118), were officially named in 2016.

items.title: Diamond and graphite
items.body: Diamond and graphite (the 'lead' in pencils) are both pure carbon. The only difference is how the carbon atoms are arranged, which makes one the hardest natural material and the other soft.

items.title: What air is made of
items.body: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and nearly 1% argon. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%, but it has a big effect on the climate.

items.title: 86 billion neurons
items.body: The human brain contains roughly 86 billion nerve cells (neurons), connected by trillions of synapses. It uses about 20% of the body's energy while making up only about 2% of body weight.

items.title: How vaccines work
items.body: A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise a germ, using a harmless part or weakened form of it. If the real germ arrives later, the body can fight it faster.

items.title: The cell's power plants
items.body: Mitochondria produce most of the chemical energy a cell uses, in the form of a molecule called ATP. They have their own small set of DNA, inherited from the mother.

items.title: Around Earth in 90 minutes
items.body: The International Space Station travels at about 28,000 km/h and circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes, so astronauts on board see about 16 sunrises a day.

items.title: Moore's law
items.body: In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling regularly; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years. This trend drove decades of faster, cheaper computers.

items.title: Absolute zero
items.body: Absolute zero, −273.15 °C (0 kelvin), is the lowest possible temperature, where particles have the least possible energy. Scientists have cooled matter to within billionths of a degree of it.

items.title: Newton's first law
items.body: An object stays still, or keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless a force acts on it. This is inertia. It is why passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly.

items.title: A light-year is a distance
items.body: A light-year is how far light travels in one year: about 9.46 trillion km. It measures distance, not time. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

items.title: Inside an atom
items.body: An atom has a tiny nucleus of protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge), surrounded by electrons (negative). The number of protons decides which element it is: 6 protons is always carbon.

items.title: The pH scale
items.body: pH measures how acidic or alkaline a liquid is, usually from 0 to 14. 7 is neutral (pure water). Below 7 is acidic, like lemon juice; above 7 is alkaline, like soap.

items.title: The greenhouse effect
items.body: Gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour let sunlight in but trap some of the heat Earth gives off. Without it, Earth would be far too cold for life; more of these gases warm the planet further.

items.title: Science word: catalyst
items.body: Meaning: a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. Enzymes are catalysts in living things.
items.example_sentence: Enzymes in saliva act as a catalyst to break down starch.

items.title: Science word: osmosis
items.body: Meaning: the movement of water through a membrane from a weaker solution to a stronger one.
items.example_sentence: Plant roots take in water by osmosis.

items.title: Science word: hypothesis
items.body: Meaning: a proposed explanation that can be tested by experiment or observation.
items.example_sentence: Her hypothesis was that plants grow faster with music.

items.title: Light versus sound
items.body: Physics check.
items.statement: Sound travels faster than light
items.explanation: Light moves at about 300,000 km per second; sound in air at about 0.34 km per second. That is why you see lightning before you hear thunder.

items.title: Counting bones
items.body: Human body check.
items.statement: An adult human usually has 206 bones
items.explanation: Adults usually have 206 bones. Babies have more, around 270, and many fuse as they grow.

items.title: Antibiotics and colds
items.body: Health check.
items.statement: Antibiotics cure viral infections like the common cold
items.explanation: Colds and flu are caused by viruses. Antibiotics only work on bacteria, and misusing them causes resistance.

items.title: Our Sun
items.body: Space check.
items.statement: The Sun is a star
items.explanation: The Sun is a medium-sized star, a huge ball of hot gas powered by nuclear fusion.

items.title: Cooking on a mountain
items.body: Physics check.
items.statement: Water boils at a lower temperature high on a mountain
items.explanation: Lower air pressure at altitude lowers the boiling point. On Everest water boils at about 70 °C.

items.title: Hottest planet check
items.body: Space check.
items.statement: Mercury is the hottest planet in our solar system
items.explanation: Venus is hotter (about 465 °C) because its thick atmosphere traps heat, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

items.title: What diamonds are made of
items.body: Chemistry check.
items.statement: Diamonds are made of carbon
items.explanation: Diamond is pure carbon with its atoms locked in a very strong 3D pattern.

items.title: The main gas in air
items.body: Earth science check.
items.statement: Oxygen is the most common gas in Earth's air
items.explanation: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.

items.title: Are bats birds?
items.body: Biology check.
items.statement: Bats are mammals
items.explanation: Bats have fur, give birth to live young and feed them milk. They are the only mammals capable of true flight.

items.title: Lightning myths
items.body: Weather check.
items.statement: Lightning never strikes the same place twice
items.explanation: Tall structures are hit again and again. New York's Empire State Building is struck many times every year.
